title: A Dream Seen in the Glare of Publicity!
translatorNote: This translation is intended to carry Kalaignar's voice into clear, contemporary English rather than recast the letter as literary or academic prose. It preserves the source's argument, political directness, rhetorical questions, repetition, irony, factual detail, and paragraph order. Names, dates, figures, quotations, and intentional English expressions are retained. Where Tamil idiom cannot be reproduced literally without sounding unnatural, the English follows its sense and rhetorical force without adding claims absent from the source. The original Tamil is reproduced in full below the translation and remains the authoritative text. `Udanpirappē` is retained in Tamil transliteration rather than flattened into “brother,” “sister,” or “comrade.” Literally evoking “one born alongside me,” Kalaignar uses it as a distinctive address of shared identity, equality, affection, and solidarity within the movement.
paragraphs: At a time when power cuts continue in Tamil Nadu because of an electricity shortage, reports say that 5.73 crore units generated by windmills were wasted in just the last ten days. After a gap of a few weeks, reports that power cuts may resume across the State have again begun to frighten and alarm the public.

Wind-power producers have now filed a case alleging that the Tamil Nadu Government refuses to purchase fifty per cent of the electricity they generate. In an interview, Indian Wind Power Association President Mr Kasturi Rangaiyan said that India ranked fifth in the world in installed wind-power capacity, with windmills capable of producing 19,500 megawatts, forty per cent of them in Tamil Nadu. The Government had assured anyone establishing windmills in Tamil Nadu that all the electricity generated would be purchased. Trusting that assurance, entrepreneurs installed large numbers of windmills and produced power. Until June, everything proceeded properly. The Government and the Electricity Board were now refusing to purchase their electricity, causing severe losses.

He explained that the producers had borrowed nearly seventy per cent of the cost of the windmills from banks, believing that the Government would buy the electricity. How could they survive if the State suddenly refused to take the power? He attributed the decision to the purchase of electricity from other States. Wind power was being supplied at only ₹3.05 a unit, while electricity purchased from outside Tamil Nadu cost ₹4.91, with an additional transmission charge of ₹1.20—₹6.11 a unit in all. By rejecting wind power and buying from outside at twice the price, the Electricity Board only increased its losses. Tamil Nadu, once first in India in wind-power production, had fallen to fifth place, and the State Government was responsible. Producers had met officials, ministers and the Chief Minister's Office without obtaining a solution. Only after waiting patiently for two months had they approached the court.

However, a supervising engineer of the Tamil Nadu Transmission Corporation, Kaliyaperumal, wrote to Junior Vikatan claiming that Kasturi Rangaiyan's statement that wind power was not being purchased was incorrect.

In a further statement issued on 18 September 2013, Association President Professor Kasturi Rangaiyan said the Tamil Nadu Electricity Board was refusing to purchase locally produced wind power because it was buying thermal power from other States. During the windy season from June to August, windmills had been prevented from operating for as much as twenty-two hours a day. Such treatment would place the future of wind power in doubt. Advanced countries increasingly used clean wind energy rather than polluting coal-based thermal power, and Tamil Nadu too should continue to use wind power properly.
The Association and the State Government must therefore explain the real situation clearly to the confused public.
Meanwhile, because of the power-cut crisis, streetlights fail to burn at night in many parts of Chennai itself. Reports continue that factories across Coimbatore are suffering heavily.

This week's India Today carried a special article on the power cuts. At its beginning, A. Vasudevan, who operated a lathe workshop in Coimbatore's Idaiyarpalayam area, said he did not have the courage to take his own life as others had done, while pride kept him from weeping before strangers. Power cuts prevented him from completing work on time. Where he once received orders worth as much as ₹5 lakh a month, he now struggled to obtain even ₹10,000 worth.

J. James, district secretary of the Tamil Nadu Cottage and Tiny Industries Association, said large firms had shifted orders previously given to Coimbatore's small and micro enterprises to China and elsewhere because those units could not withstand the power crisis. The small-industries sector faced severe destruction. In the previous six months alone, the effects of the crisis had reportedly driven 350 people in the Coimbatore region to suicide. Unlike large companies, small enterprises could not run generators. Their orders had therefore moved elsewhere. Nearly 6,000 small and micro units had closed, leaving 60,000 people without work. Many who lost their jobs were surviving by driving autos, selling appalams or taking daily-wage work elsewhere.

During the 2011 general election, the AIADMK manifesto promised: “Darkened Tamil Nadu will be made radiant. Rapid action will be taken to supply uninterrupted electricity needed for homes, industries and agriculture. Immediately after the All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam assumes office, a special scheme will be implemented for this purpose.” After coming to power, the rulers contented themselves with describing two years of achievements in four-page advertisements. But what is the real situation? Has darkened Tamil Nadu been made bright—or has a once-bright Tamil Nadu been turned into darkness?
The Times of India of 13 September 2013 reported:
The regular power cuts, extending to 20 hours a day in some districts, in the last fiscal year kept many investors away from Tamil Nadu
It further stated:
Last year, the power problem was severe and many small and medium scale industries went out of business. This is the main reason for the State losing many big investments
The comment was attributed to D.S. Rawat, National Secretary General of Assocham.

Investment in new industries stood at 5.7 per cent in the 2011–2012 financial year, but had fallen sharply to 1.8 per cent in the current year. A Reserve Bank report released on the 10th of the month placed Tamil Nadu eighth and last in its ranking. While investment in new industries across India totalled ₹1.96 lakh crore, Tamil Nadu's share was only ₹3,533 crore, the report said.

Before the AIADMK came to power, what did Jayalalithaa tell public meetings? Did she not promise to eliminate power cuts within three months? Not three months but two and a half years had passed. What was the position now?

Responding to the debate on the Governor's Address after assuming office in 2011, Chief Minister Jayalalithaa said the existing three-hour power cut would be reduced to two hours and that Tamil Nadu's electricity shortage would be completely resolved from July that year. In an interview to India Today in February 2012, the Electricity Minister said Tamil Nadu would experience shortage only between March and May 2012 and that, if people bore those three months, there would thereafter be no shortage.

When I raised this issue the previous year, Jayalalithaa told the Assembly she had never promised to repair Tamil Nadu's power-cut situation within three months. I immediately replied in Murasoli on 6 November 2012 that Dina Thanthi had published her response to the Governor's Address debate on 10 June 2011 and that it contained her promise to reduce the three-hour cut to two hours. After that, as with many other issues, she simply abandoned the subject.

The Government later approached the Supreme Court seeking a direction to the Union Government to supply Tamil Nadu with approximately 1,900 megawatts of surplus power held by Delhi. The Union Government said it could not provide it. The truth was that, even if the power were supplied, there was no transmission corridor to bring it to Tamil Nadu. When I pointed this out, they asked why the DMK Government had not created such a corridor. I then cited their own 2012–2013 Budget Statement, which admitted that congestion in the transmission system prevented electricity available in other States from being brought into Tamil Nadu. After that, they fell silent.

In an Assembly announcement on 25 April 2013, the Chief Minister read out promise after promise: a ₹7,000-crore hydroelectric project in the Nilgiris; ₹5,000 crore to strengthen the grid and transmission network; nineteen new 400-kilovolt substations costing ₹3,572 crore; a ₹1,000-crore substation and transmission lines at Tiruvalam; and projects worth ₹30,602 crore to make Tamil Nadu power-surplus once again. What stage have any of them reached?

Villages still endure more than fifteen hours of power cuts. Children cannot sleep at night without air, and parents carry them into the streets. Factories across Coimbatore, Tiruppur and Erode have closed, workers have lost their livelihoods and wander in search of food, and many thousands have moved to neighbouring States seeking work. Do these rulers care about any of it?

The condition of electricity supply under this Government can be understood from an order issued on 26 November 2012 by a Division Bench comprising Chief Justice M.Y. Eqbal and Justice T.S. Sivagnanam. The judges recorded that electricity was reportedly supplied for only a few hours a day in many districts and was cut for more than twelve hours daily in Coimbatore and elsewhere. They directed the Tamil Nadu Electricity Board to file a detailed report stating the duration of cuts in each district and to explain why the timings were not announced to the public in advance through the media. Are those judicial observations not enough to understand the condition of the power sector?

Every day the newspapers report that one generating station has stopped here and another has stopped there. After taking office, the AIADMK Government failed to accelerate the generating projects begun under the DMK Government. It has also shown confusion and hesitation in purchasing and distributing private wind power. Because solving the electricity crisis has not been given priority, public suffering has not diminished; production in small industries has fallen sharply; the plight of lakhs of unemployed workers brings tears to the eyes; investors turn away at the mention of Tamil Nadu; and industrial growth has withered. Time passes only amid flex boards, banners, posters and full-page newspaper advertisements. Taken as a whole, the AIADMK rulers are dreaming in the glare of publicity.
With affection, M.K. 24 September 2013
